clue.text: Is this just for dippers and divers?

definitions.text: Is this just for dippers and divers?

parts.words: Is this just for dippers and divers?
parts.note: dippers and divers sound like swimmers at a pool, but they are birds, and the question asks what garden fixture exists for birds to splash in

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a facility is reserved for swimmers who dip and dive.
explanation.walkthrough: A dipper is a small bird that bobs and dives in streams, and many birds dip into water; the clue dresses birds up as bathers.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden basin of water put out so that small birds can drink and wash.

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship
chat means talk

explanation.surface: Insolence calls for a severe telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stern' looks like an adjective meaning severe, but it is the rear of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheeky retorts, the insolent answering back of a pert child.

indicators.note: generating means producing something new from the material, here a reworking of the letters
initially means only the opening letter is used

explanation.surface: An electrical transformer produces enormous energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'generating' rearranges TERRIFIC plus E, the first letter of 'energy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A device converting alternating current to direct current, so one that changes electricity.

explanation.surface: A call to shun a dance held by pottery workers.
explanation.walkthrough: Potters here are snooker players, who pot balls; their black ball is worth most. Geoffrey Boycott, a Yorkshire cricketer, adds a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: To blacklist something means to ban it, and in snooker the most valuable coloured ball is so named.

clue.text: He will have marked cards, of course

definitions.text: He will have marked cards, of course

parts.words: He will have marked cards, of course
parts.note: marked cards hint at a cheat, but the cards are race cards and of course means at the racecourse

explanation.surface: A card sharp naturally plays with doctored cards.
explanation.walkthrough: A race card lists the runners at a meeting; a man giving betting advice marks his selections on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sells or offers betting advice on horse races.

explanation.surface: A sprite is discovered tucked away in a nook.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobweb is one of Titania's fairy attendants in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairy servant in Shakespeare's play bears this name, and spiders spin such webs in neglected room corners.

indicators.note: exploded means the letters are blown apart and come down in a new order

explanation.surface: Ammunition for a French army rifle blew up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploded' rearranges RIFLEAMMO.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-gold banner of the medieval French kings, carried into battle.

parts.note: a bad speller seems to be someone weak at spelling, but here it is someone casting wicked spells

explanation.surface: A person who cannot spell properly.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorceress who casts spells, often evil ones.

clue.text: Graduate gets measure of fine horse.

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
a yard is a measure of length

explanation.surface: A graduate measures out a superb horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Bayard was the magical bay horse of medieval romance.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary steed of Renaud in the Charlemagne romances, so a famous horse.

indicators.note: some means only part of these letters is taken

explanation.surface: A partly superfluous translator of an early English historian.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run inside 'half-redundant'. King Alfred the Great is credited with an Old English version of Bede's Ecclesiastical History.
explanation.definitionFit: King Alfred of Wessex sponsored and is credited with an Old English rendering of Bede's history.

clue.text: Merger of firms by a Chestertonian cad

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm; a merger joins two of them
the second company in the merger, again CO

explanation.surface: A company merger is engineered by a rotter out of a G. K. Chesterton story.
explanation.walkthrough: G. K. Chesterton's poem The Song of Right and Wrong declares that this drink 'is a cad and coward'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's verse insults the chocolate drink as a vulgar bounder, so it is his literary cad.

clue.text: One's essay gets first prize for handy reading

indicators.note: gets first tells us the word for prize is placed at the front, ahead of the other pieces

parts.note: the palm is a symbol of victory, so a prize
One's is read as one is, I + S, written IS
an essay is an attempt, a try

explanation.surface: A student's essay wins top prize for skilful reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handy reading' is reading of the hand, not adept reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune-telling by studying the lines on a person's hand.

parts.note: the hymn title hides W. G. Grace, the great Victorian batsman, so the player is one of his sport rather than a musician

explanation.surface: A musician performs the well-known hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace was England's most famous nineteenth-century player of the bat-and-ball game; 'amazing' fits him as well as the hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: W. G. Grace is the classic example of a player of the English bat-and-ball sport.

indicators.note: a scrummage is a jumbled struggle, so the letters are mixed up
first-half means only the opening half of the team's name is used

explanation.surface: A musician turns out in a rugby scrum during the first half of a Harlequins match.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of HARLEQUINS is HARLE, which 'scrummage' rearranges. Harlequins is a London rugby club; Franz Lehár wrote The Merry Widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehár was the Hungarian writer of operettas such as The Merry Widow.

clue.text: An old way to right daring young man

parts.note: via is the Latin word for road, the way of the ancient Romans

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned route to correct a reckless youth.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition echoes the song about 'the daring young man on the flying trapeze'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot is a bold flier, as in the song's young man who flies through the air.

explanation.surface: A final memorial stands in the American desert.
explanation.walkthrough: Tombstone is a Wild West town in Arizona, home of the gunfight at the O.K. Corral.
explanation.definitionFit: A grave marker is the final memorial to someone, and an Arizona town bears the name.

clue.text: Domino's first with a disguise in reversible fabric

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of Domino is taken

parts.note: a mask is a disguise for the face

explanation.surface: A masked reveller in a domino arrives first in disguise, wearing reversible cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: A domino is a hooded cloak worn with a mask at masquerades, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a woven cloth whose pattern shows on both sides, so it can be turned over.

clue.text: The trick is to serve up a variety of game-pies.

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for pies is read from bottom to top

parts.note: tarts are pies

indicators.note: a variety of means the letters of game are mixed

explanation.surface: The secret is to offer an assortment of game pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'serve up' turns TARTS into STRAT; 'a variety of' rearranges GAME as AGEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruse or clever scheme devised to outwit someone.

explanation.surface: Making money out of a pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Money earned on a loan or investment, and a pastime that holds one's attention.

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that the greedy schoolboy has eaten almost everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the gluttonous schoolboy of British boys' stories, famous for scoffing every bun in sight.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of surprise, and the tiny scraps a glutton leaves behind on the plate.

clue.text: What affects hock and burgundy, perhaps? Mineral water on top!

indicators.note: on top means that in this down clue the spa goes above the wine

parts.note: spa water is mineral water
burgundy is an example of wine, vin in French

explanation.surface: A drinker asks what ruins hock and burgundy, then tops them with mineral water.
explanation.walkthrough: Hock looks like the German wine beside burgundy, but it is the joint in a horse's hind leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A swelling of the hock joint in horses, causing lameness.

clue.text: In tears, perhaps, from what is in soap

indicators.note: perhaps means the letters might be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: Someone weeping over what goes into soap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IN and TEARS together.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatty compound, the glyceride of stearic acid, used in soap and candle making.

clue.text: Board shows one run with an hour's interruption

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into something, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: in cricket a single is one run
H is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: A scoreboard displays a single run after an hour's break in play.
explanation.walkthrough: A single is a cricket score of one run.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle is a thin wooden tile, a board used on roofs and walls.

parts.note: suggests an infantryman of the Great War, but this soldier digs the trenches

explanation.surface: An infantryman serves at the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: A sap is a trench dug toward the enemy, and the Royal Engineers' private soldiers are known by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A military engineer who digs saps, the trenches and tunnels of siege warfare.

indicators.note: curtailed means the tail, the final letter, is cut off

parts.note: at last means finally

explanation.surface: An American weapons programme is at last cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' drops the last letter of AT LAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlas was an early American intercontinental rocket, later a space launcher.

parts.note: la is French for the
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: The French are able to speak out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'give tongue' looks like a phrase meaning speak, but 'give' is only a link and 'tongue' means language.
explanation.definitionFit: A tongue is a language, here the speech of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Haughty type let loose as a peripatetic teacher

parts.note: an aristo, short for aristocrat, is a lofty type

indicators.note: let loose means the letters of let are set free to rearrange

explanation.surface: A snooty person is turned loose as a wandering tutor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges LET as TLE. The Greek philosopher taught while walking, and his school was called the Peripatetics.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher lectured while strolling in the Lyceum, giving his followers the name Peripatetic.

clue.text: Nasal quality as from Bow, say

explanation.surface: Someone speaks with a nasal East London accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an East London district, suggesting a Cockney accent, but here it is the archer's bow whose string sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasal tone of voice, and the ringing sound of a plucked string such as a bowstring.

clue.text: Post Office in Scotland suffering from underground activity

parts.note: to thole is the Scots word for to endure, so suffering is tholing there

explanation.surface: A Scottish post office is struggling because of clandestine goings-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'underground activity' suggests subversion, but it means exploring caves.
explanation.definitionFit: Caving: exploring deep shafts and caves beneath the surface.

explanation.surface: Someone asks what an ancestor's point of view might have been.
explanation.walkthrough: The Angles were a Germanic people who settled in England, so possible forebears of the English.
explanation.definitionFit: A viewpoint or perspective, and a member of a tribe from which the English descend.

explanation.surface: A question about youth movement members.
explanation.walkthrough: Rovers were senior Scouts and Rangers are senior Guides, so the clue looks like a choice between two movements.
explanation.definitionFit: One who roams as a wanderer, and a senior member of the Girl Guides.

clue.text: Fruit embargo for revision starting tomorrow

indicators.note: for revision means the letters are to be revised into a new order
starting means just the opening letter is used

explanation.surface: A trade ban on fruit is to be revised, effective tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for revision' rearranges EMBARGO as BERGAMO, then add the first letter of 'tomorrow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A citrus fruit, the bergamot orange, whose oil flavours Earl Grey tea.
